endorsements.quote: Accordingly, pediatric AI programs should establish governance processes (e.g., algorithm review committees) that include clinical, data science, ethics, and family or community perspectives to review intended use, consent communication, and accountability when errors occur ( Vaccaro et al., 2024 ; Gorski and Rudloff, 2023 ).

Critically, readiness should include explicit deprecation and decommissioning/retirement criteria (e.g., performance drift, guideline changes, equity harms, and vendor changes) and a plan for safe transition to an updated tool or non-AI workflow.

Readiness includes standardized performance evaluation (e.g., discrimination, calibration, and clinically meaningful utility), age-stratified and subgroup analyses, and external validation across settings.
Human factors testing with clinicians and, when relevant, caregivers and adolescents should assess usability, comprehension, and conditions under which users override or over-rely on AI.

From an AI governance perspective, transparency includes documenting model purpose, intended users, training data provenance, performance across relevant pediatric subgroups, and known failure modes ( Center for Devices, Radiological Health, 2024 ).

This includes budget impact and cost-effectiveness considerations where appropriate, resource requirements for integration and support, and lifecycle plans for monitoring, retraining, version control, and rollback.

Readiness includes the transparent documentation of dataset provenance and limitations; reporting of model performance across pediatric developmental strata relevant to the intended use (e.g., neonatal, infant, child, and adolescent); and disaggregation by key demographic and social determinants where feasible.

unlisted_practices: Establish clinician override pathways so licensed clinicians can override or disregard AI outputs.
Use formal override prompts to counter automation bias.
Implement validation checks that AI-generated text matches source data.
Use note templates for AI documentation that preserve family concerns and developmental goals.
Inform families when AI meaningfully influences care, seeking developmentally appropriate assent when feasible.
Address parent-proxy access and adolescent confidentiality in pediatric AI deployment.
Include family participatory co-design in low-resource adaptable AI tools.
Assess lifecycle costs, and environmental footprint of AI tools.

screen.reason: Introduces a pediatric-focused implementation-readiness checklist and governance framework (the PAIR framework) for planning, evaluating, and operationalizing AI tools.
